name: Adam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the cattle and the grass at Wagner's, which is my uncle's farm. A hundred and forty suckler cows, that's cows that rear their own calves for beef, and about two hundred hectares of grass, most of which I make into hay and sell. In winter the cows are in the sheds, so I'm feeding by seven, checking the bulling heifers, and then I'm in the workshop getting the baler ready for spring. I've got one lad full-time, Ben, and my uncle still comes out to argue with me about everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your uncle argue about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly the money I spend. Two years ago I bought a second-hand big baler on finance, sixty thousand, because I wanted to bale for the neighbours as a contractor. He thought I'd lost my mind. It's paying for itself, just, but it's why we've got less than a month in the bank. I'd do it again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you organise all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my phone, mostly. I use an AI tool every day, it books the contracting jobs, reads the weather models and tells me which day's best to cut, keeps the cattle records. It wrote my last grant application in an evening when it used to take me a week. My uncle calls it my girlfriend. Lucy, my wife, doesn't find that as funny as he does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like June, when the hay's cut and turned and it smells right, and you're baling till eleven at night with the lights on. It's my best month for money too. What wears me out is the paperwork from the government. Ear tags, movement forms, inspections, grant rules that change every year. I'd rather spend that time with Jack and Evie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best tool I've bought, and it was nearly free. I'd tell every farmer at the mart to use it, and some of them would. The old ones wouldn't, and that's their choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, honestly. I'm already using it every day. If it gets a bit better and nothing else changes, I get a few more hours a week and I can grow the contracting side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on more contracting jobs, maybe ten more farms next summer, booked and planned through the app. I'd pay Ben more for the overtime. I might look at a second-hand tedder, the machine that turns the hay, to keep up, about eight thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like the first fine week in June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Another eight thousand on finance, with less than a month saved. Does that ever worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some nights, yes. But my grandfather bought this farm with a loan nobody thought he'd pay back, and he did. You don't build anything by sitting on your hands waiting for the bank to like you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucy say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say ask her first next time, which is fair. She's careful with money, she runs the books from her salon. We're a good pair, I push and she pulls me back.

S0.say: I'd say it's the best tool I've bought and it was nearly free. I'd tell every farmer at the mart to use it, and the older ones who wouldn't could make their own choice.
S0.think: I think it's good for me, since I already use it daily. If it improves and nothing else changes, I gain hours each week and can grow the contracting side.
S0.do: Takes on about ten more contracting farms next summer, planned through the AI app, pays his worker Ben more overtime, and considers a second-hand hay tedder for about eight thousand on finance.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the first fine week in June.
S0.quote: You don't build anything by sitting on your hands waiting for the bank to like you.
S0.fieldNote: He's an enthusiastic risk-taker who links his borrowing to his grandfather's story. His traditional values show as family pride and self-reliance rather than suspicion of new tools. His wife acts as the brake, and he says so happily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the market sort it out at its own pace. People who use the tools will do well, people who don't will fall behind, and that's always been the way. But I'd also say firms should take on young people properly, apprenticeships, not just sit back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think slow suits me down to the ground. I'm ahead of most farmers round here with the tools already. If it takes ten years, I've got ten years to build the contracting business before anyone catches up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on an apprentice, a young lad or lass from the agricultural college, for the contracting work. That's maybe twelve thousand a year with the grant. I'd also try to get the AI to plan baling routes across all my customers, so I'm not driving the baler up and down the same lane twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who don't use the tools will fall behind. Does that include your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, and I love him, and he knows. He's seventy-four and he's done his bit. He'd say that's exactly why he leaves the computer stuff to me. We get on fine, as long as I don't tell him how to fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprentice costs money. Why take that on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody took me on. Old Harold the contractor let me drive his tractor at fifteen and paid me in cash and bacon sandwiches. If farmers don't train young people, who will? Not the government, that's for sure.

S1.say: I'd say let the market sort it out at its own pace, as people who use the tools do well and others fall behind. But firms should still take on young people through proper apprenticeships.
S1.think: I think slow suits me perfectly because I'm already ahead of most local farmers with the tools. Ten years gives me time to build the contracting business before others catch up.
S1.do: Takes on an apprentice from the agricultural college for contracting work at about twelve thousand a year after the grant, and uses AI to plan baling routes across all his customers.
S1.quote: Old Harold the contractor let me drive his tractor at fifteen and paid me in cash and bacon sandwiches.
S1.fieldNote: He sees a slow rollout as a head start for himself. His free-market views sit beside a strong sense of duty to train young people, which he puts on farmers rather than government. The affection for his uncle came through clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people losing office jobs should look at trades and farming, there's work if you'll get your hands dirty. I don't think the government paying people to sit at home helps anyone. Retraining, fine, if it's for real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not my problem directly, and that's the honest truth. But Lucy's salon depends on office women in town getting their hair done every six weeks. If they lose their jobs, they go every twelve weeks, and that's half her money. That bit worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucy to start a list of farm wives and older ladies who aren't affected, and build that side. I'd offer office people a day's work on the farm at haymaking, a few of them would like it. And I'd try one of the new AI-related jobs myself, maybe teaching other farmers to use the tools, a couple of evenings a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the farm, a bit uneasy about Lucy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching other farmers. Would they listen to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger ones would. I already show people at the mart. I'd charge forty for an evening, run it in the back room of the pub, bring my laptop, and show them how I book my baling. Half of them would come for the beer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government paying people doesn't help. What about Lucy, if her salon struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate taking anything, same as me. We'd tighten up, we'd ask my uncle for a bit of the hay money, and we'd ride it out. That's what families are for.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs should look at trades and farming, where there's work if you'll get your hands dirty. Government paying people to sit at home helps nobody, though retraining for real jobs is fine.
S2.think: I think it's not directly my problem. But my wife's salon depends on office women having their hair done every six weeks, and if they lose jobs that drops to twelve, halving her income.
S2.do: Helps his wife build a client list of people less affected, offers office workers paid days at haymaking, and starts teaching other farmers AI tools in the pub back room at about forty an evening.
S2.feel: Calm about the farm, a bit uneasy about his wife's business.
S2.quote: I'd charge forty for an evening, run it in the back room of the pub, bring my laptop, and show them how I book my baling.
S2.fieldNote: His first instinct is entrepreneurial: turn the disruption into a side business. The honest admission that it's not his problem was quickly followed by real worry about his wife's salon. He'd rather lean on family than on state help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who own shares earned the right to them, and if you didn't buy any, that's your choice. But I'd also say a country can't hold together if half the people are out of work. The answer is getting people working, building houses, not taking money off people who saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right, physical work is untouched. But land and house prices booming is bad for me. My uncle wants to retire, and I've always hoped to buy the farm from him one day. If land jumps, I'll never afford it, and some city investor buys it for a tax break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle in the first month and ask him to sell me the farm, or set up a deal now, before prices go any higher. I'd talk to the bank, though with our savings they'd laugh at me. I'd also try to get more contracting work from the bigger estates, whose owners would have more money than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the first time I've felt the ground move under the farm itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Asking your uncle to sell to you, how would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, probably. He'd say he's got to think of my cousins too, his daughters. They live in the city and they'd want the money. That's the bit nobody likes to talk about at Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if you didn't buy shares, that's your choice. You didn't buy any. Was that your choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I put everything into the baler and the cattle. That was my choice too, and I'd still say it was the right one. But yes, I'd be on the wrong side of that boom, and I'd know it.

S3.say: I'd say shareholders earned their gains, and not buying shares is your own choice. But a country can't hold together with half its people out of work, so the answer is jobs and house building, not taking savers' money.
S3.think: I think I'm all right because physical work is untouched. But booming land prices would end my hope of buying the farm from my uncle, and a city investor might buy it for a tax break.
S3.do: Asks his uncle in the first month to sell him the farm or agree a deal before prices rise further, approaches the bank despite thin savings, and chases more contracting work from wealthy estates.
S3.feel: Uneasy, feeling the ground move under the farm for the first time.
S3.quote: I put everything into the baler and the cattle. That was my choice too, and I'd still say it was the right one.
S3.fieldNote: When I pointed out that he hadn't bought shares either, he accepted it without getting defensive, which was striking. His real fear here is family inheritance: cousins in the city wanting their share of a now-valuable farm. This was the first scenario where he looked worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are coming whether we like it or not, so farmers should own them, not rent them from big companies. Give us the tax breaks to buy them and the freedom to use them. I'd say that loudly at the farmers' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think hay's one of the first things robots do well. Self-driving mowers, robot balers, they're nearly there already. If every farmer can buy a robot baler, nobody needs a contractor, and my business is gone. The cattle side's safer, but not much, feeding robots exist already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to be the robot contractor instead of the man with the tractor. I'd look at buying one robot mower on finance, maybe in the first year, and selling my baler while it's still worth something. And I'd sit down with Lucy and draw up a plan for if it doesn't work, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm still moving, but it's the first time I could see it all going wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd borrow again, for a robot, with under a month saved. Is that brave or reckless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. Lucy would say reckless. But if I stand still, I lose the business for certain. If I jump, I might lose it, or I might be the one everyone calls. I know which I'd rather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jack, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the farm's still here, and he can still farm, but he'll need to know the machines inside out. Jack already fixes the quad bike with me. I'd tell him the farmer of the future is half mechanic, half cowman, and all stubborn.

S4.say: I'd say robots are coming regardless, so farmers should own them rather than rent from big companies. Give us tax breaks to buy them and freedom to use them, and I'd say it loudly at the farmers' union.
S4.think: I think hay-making is one of the first jobs robots will do well, and if every farmer can buy a robot baler my contracting business is gone. The cattle side is safer, but not by much.
S4.do: Aims to become a robot contractor, considering buying a robot mower on finance in the first year and selling his baler while it holds value. Sits down with his wife to make a fallback plan for the first time.
S4.feel: Anxious but still moving, seeing for the first time how it could all go wrong.
S4.quote: I'd tell him the farmer of the future is half mechanic, half cowman, and all stubborn.
S4.fieldNote: Even here his answer was to borrow and jump, though he admitted it might be reckless. The new step was agreeing to make a fallback plan with his wife. His traditional pride in the family farm and his love of new tools sit together without friction.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because they could take the contracting business I've built from nothing in two years. What would help is fair access to finance for small farmers to buy the machines themselves, so it isn't just the big companies who own them. And less paperwork, so I can spend my time farming, not filling forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about inheritance. On a family farm, the biggest question isn't robots or AI, it's who gets the land when the old man goes. All this would make that harder, and that's where families fall out.

headlineQuote: If I jump, I might lose it, or I might be the one everyone calls. I know which I'd rather.
portrait: Adam Wagner, 43, runs the beef cattle and hay on his uncle's farm and has built a hay-baling contracting business on a sixty-thousand finance deal, leaving the family with under a month in the bank. He uses AI every day for bookings, weather and records, and loves new tools as much as he loves his grandfather's story of building the farm on a risky loan. His free-market, family-first views lead him to apprenticeships and family help rather than state support. He stays calm and entrepreneurial through most scenarios, worrying more about his wife's salon and buying the farm from his uncle, until robots threaten the contracting business itself.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because robot mowers and balers could wipe out the contracting business he has built in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to finance so small farmers can own the machines themselves, and less government paperwork.
